content: Cullin 1, commonly referred to as CUL1, is a protein encoded by the CUL1 gene in humans and is a member of the cullin protein family. This protein is integral to the regulation of protein degradation and ubiquitination processes. Specifically, CUL1 is a critical component of the SCF (SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, which facilitates the ubiquitination of target proteins involved in essential cellular processes such as cell cycle progression, signal transduction, and transcriptional regulation. Within the SCF complex, CUL1 functions as a structural scaffold, providing a rigid framework that organizes the SKP1-F-box protein and RBX1 subunits. This structural role is essential for the proper positioning of the substrate and the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, thereby contributing to the catalytic activity of the complex. The SCF complex typically consists of CUL1, RBX1, SKP1, and SKP2, and CUL1 also interacts with other proteins such as RNF7. Additionally, CUL1 is part of a larger complex that includes TIP120A/CAND1 and RBX1. In its unneddylated form, CUL1 interacts with TIP120A/CAND1, which negatively regulates its association with SKP1 within the SCF complex. CUL1 also interacts with COPS2. CUL1 is expressed in lung fibroblasts and undergoes post-translational modification through neddylation, a process that enhances the ubiquitination activity of the SCF complex. Conversely, CUL1 can be deneddylated through its interaction with the COP9 signalosome (CSN) complex, which modulates its activity. This protein has been extensively studied in the context of its role in cell cycle regulation and protein turnover, with numerous studies highlighting its interactions with other proteins and its functional importance in maintaining cellular homeostasis.
